subtopic_detail: initial conservative management of urinary urgency when stress leakage and infection have been excluded
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58 year old woman with eight months of a sudden compelling need to pass urine that she struggles to defer. She gets up four times most nights and has twice not made it to the toilet in time.

She tells you she does not leak when she coughs, laughs or lifts her grandchildren, and that the problem is entirely about the urgency. She drinks six cups of coffee across the day and a glass of wine most evenings. She has had two vaginal births and her last period was at 52. She has no haematuria, no dysuria and no pelvic pain. Her examination and investigations are complete.

data_table.Examination: Mild vaginal atrophy, no prolapse beyond the hymen on Valsalva, no leakage demonstrated on cough stress testing, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, midstream urine culture no growth, post void residual volume 30 mL on bladder scan, fasting glucose within normal limits, bladder diary shows nine voids by day and four by night with small volumes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Bladder training with caffeine reduction and pelvic floor exercises
options.rationale: Behavioural treatment is first line for urinary urgency and produces improvement rates comparable to drug therapy without adverse effects. Bladder training progressively extends the interval between voids, and her six cups of coffee daily represent a substantial and readily modifiable bladder irritant. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Oral oxybutynin with review of the symptoms in six weeks time
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy is second line after behavioural measures have been tried, and oxybutynin specifically has the highest anticholinergic burden of the available agents, with cumulative exposure linked to cognitive decline in older women. If a drug were indicated, a more selective agent would be preferred. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Oral mirabegron with review of the blood pressure in six weeks
options.rationale: A beta 3 agonist avoids the anticholinergic burden and is a sound pharmacological choice for this condition, so the drug itself is not the error. It still belongs after a trial of behavioural treatment rather than instead of one. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Referral for urodynamic studies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Urodynamic testing is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, mixed or complicated symptoms, or failure of initial treatment, and it is invasive and uncomfortable. Her history, bladder diary, negative cough stress test and normal residual volume already identify the pattern. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Referral for insertion of a midurethral sling within three months
options.rationale: A sling supports the urethra and treats leakage provoked by a rise in abdominal pressure, which is the opposite mechanism to hers and which her negative cough stress test excludes. Placing a sling for urgency can worsen symptoms and cause voiding dysfunction. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom syndrome of urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia and with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of infection or other identifiable pathology. Separating it from stress incontinence matters because the treatments differ entirely, and the history plus a cough stress test usually achieves this, with mixed patterns being common and managed by treating the more bothersome component first. The initial assessment excludes the conditions that mimic it, principally urinary infection, diabetes, a pelvic mass, incomplete emptying and haematuria requiring investigation, and a three day bladder diary is the single most informative tool because it quantifies volumes, frequency and fluid intake. First line management is behavioural: bladder training to extend voiding intervals, reduction of caffeine and alcohol, sensible fluid intake and supervised pelvic floor muscle training, which together produce meaningful improvement in a majority. Pharmacotherapy follows, with selective antimuscarinics or a beta 3 agonist preferred over oxybutynin because of anticholinergic burden, and intravesical botulinum toxin or neuromodulation reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Urgency without leakage on coughing distinguishes this from stress incontinence
Exclude infection, diabetes, incomplete emptying and haematuria first
A three day bladder diary is the most informative single assessment tool
Behavioural treatment is first line and matches drug therapy for effectiveness
Avoid oxybutynin in older women because of anticholinergic cognitive burden
explanation.pearls: Cumulative anticholinergic exposure, including from oxybutynin prescribed for bladder symptoms, is associated with an increased risk of dementia in older women, which is why a beta 3 agonist or a more selective antimuscarinic is preferred once behavioural treatment has been tried.

subtopic_detail: choosing a drainage technique that reduces recurrence for an acute vulval gland abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 27 year old woman with four days of increasing pain and swelling at the right side of the vaginal opening. The pain has become severe enough that she cannot sit down properly or walk without discomfort and she did not sleep last night.

She has had no fever or rigors and is not pregnant. She has no history of a similar problem. On examination there is a tense tender swelling at the posterior aspect of the right side of the vaginal opening, about 4 cm across, which is fluctuant with thinning of the overlying skin. There is no surrounding spreading redness and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the posterior right introitus with thinned overlying skin, exquisitely tender, no surrounding cellulitis, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, speculum examination deferred because of pain
data_table.Investigations: Urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, white cell count within normal limits, C reactive protein mildly raised, sexually transmitted infection screening collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral antibiotics alone with review in the clinic in three days
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not penetrate an established collection adequately and leave the pain untreated. They are added to drainage where there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression, none of which applies here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter
options.rationale: Drainage relieves the pain immediately, and leaving a small balloon catheter in the cavity for several weeks allows an epithelialised tract to form so that the gland can continue to drain. This reduces recurrence substantially compared with drainage alone and can be done under local anaesthetic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Simple incision and drainage without any further drainage device
options.rationale: Simple drainage relieves the acute pain effectively, which is why it remains common practice, but the incision seals within days and the gland duct remains obstructed, giving recurrence rates of around a third. The catheter is what converts a temporary measure into a durable one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Marsupialisation of the cyst in theatre at the next available list
options.rationale: Marsupialisation creates a permanent drainage opening and is an effective alternative, generally reserved for recurrent disease or for failure of catheter treatment. It requires theatre and anaesthesia for a problem that can be managed today under local anaesthetic. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Needle aspiration of the contents under local anaesthetic today
options.rationale: Aspiration alone gives short lived relief because the cavity refills rapidly once the needle is withdrawn, and recurrence rates approach 100 per cent. It does not create a tract for ongoing drainage. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus and drain through short ducts into the vestibule, where obstruction produces a cyst that may be asymptomatic and require no treatment, while secondary infection produces an abscess with rapidly increasing pain over a few days. The organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a single sexually transmitted pathogen, although screening for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is appropriate because both occur. Definitive treatment is drainage combined with a technique that keeps the tract open, since the underlying problem is duct obstruction rather than infection alone, and a Word catheter left in place for two to four weeks allows epithelialisation of a new drainage tract with recurrence rates well below those of simple incision. Antibiotics are added only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, immunosuppression or a confirmed sexually transmitted pathogen. In a woman over 40, particularly with a firm or irregular mass, biopsy should be considered because carcinoma of the gland, although rare, presents in this way.
key_points: The underlying problem is duct obstruction, so drainage must keep a tract open
A Word catheter left for two to four weeks allows a new tract to epithelialise
Simple incision alone recurs in around a third of cases
Antibiotics are reserved for cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression
Consider biopsy in a woman over 40 with a firm or irregular vulval mass
explanation.pearls: A Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 that is firm, irregular or fails to resolve after drainage should be biopsied rather than simply re-drained, because adenocarcinoma of the gland presents exactly as a recurrent cyst and is easily mistaken for one.

subtopic_detail: addressing a specific factual misunderstanding before referral for a permanent method
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 31 year old woman who asks to be referred to have her tubes tied. She has three children, the youngest of whom is eight months old, and she and her partner have agreed they do not want more.

She tells you she is certain about her decision and has thought about it since her last pregnancy. When you ask what she understands about the procedure, she says she believes it can be reversed if she changes her mind later, and that she assumed it was done in a clinic room without an anaesthetic. She and her partner currently use condoms and she has not previously used any other method. She has no medical problems and takes no regular medication.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with a low transverse scar from a previous caesarean birth, no masses, body mass index 27 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test up to date and negative, urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system instead of making a referral
options.rationale: A long acting reversible method has a failure rate at least as low as tubal occlusion and should certainly be presented as an option, so the method itself is entirely reasonable. Substituting it for the procedure she has requested without discussion overrides her expressed preference. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Refer directly for laparoscopic tubal occlusion at the next clinic list
options.rationale: Referring a patient who believes the procedure is reversible and requires no anaesthetic sends her toward an operation she has not actually consented to. The misunderstanding must be corrected first, whether by you or explicitly at the specialist visit. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Provide counselling on irreversibility and the alternatives before referral
options.rationale: She holds two specific factual misunderstandings, about reversibility and about the anaesthetic required, and consent cannot be valid while they stand. Counselling covers permanence, the operative and anaesthetic risks, the failure rate with its ectopic implications, and comparison with long acting reversible methods and vasectomy, after which referral proceeds if she still wishes it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer her partner for vasectomy as the lower risk alternative procedure
options.rationale: Vasectomy is a lower risk, lower cost and more effective procedure and belongs in the discussion. Redirecting the request to a partner who is not your patient and has not been assessed bypasses her own decision making. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

options.text: Decline the request on the grounds of her age and her current parity
options.rationale: Age and parity are associated with later regret at a population level but are not grounds for refusing a competent adult's request. Refusal without counselling substitutes the clinician's judgement for the patient's. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Counselling before permanent contraception has to establish that the person understands the method is intended to be irreversible, that reversal surgery is not funded, is often unsuccessful and is not a realistic fallback, and that in vitro fertilisation is the usual route to a later pregnancy. The failure rate of tubal occlusion is roughly one in 200 over a lifetime, which is higher than many people expect and higher than that of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system or an etonogestrel implant, and a pregnancy after tubal occlusion carries a substantially increased chance of being ectopic, which is why it must be excluded promptly if a period is missed. Vasectomy should be discussed in every consultation of this kind because it is performed under local anaesthetic, has fewer complications, lower cost and a lower failure rate. Regret is more likely with younger age, lower parity, recent childbirth or relationship change, and identifying these prompts a fuller discussion rather than a refusal. Timing relative to a caesarean birth or the postpartum period is also addressed, since decisions made around delivery carry a higher rate of subsequent regret.
key_points: Valid consent requires correcting specific misunderstandings about reversibility
Lifetime failure is roughly one in 200 and a later pregnancy is often ectopic
Long acting reversible methods match or better this failure rate and are reversible
Vasectomy is lower risk, lower cost and more effective and must be discussed
Younger age and recent childbirth predict regret and prompt fuller discussion, not refusal
explanation.pearls: Any woman who misses a period after tubal occlusion needs a pregnancy test and, if positive, urgent assessment for ectopic pregnancy, because a substantial proportion of the small number of post procedure pregnancies implant outside the uterus.
